title: A Unit Called Combatives
bigQuestion: What happens to the long history of a fighting art when a school or an army packs it into a few weeks of physical training?

story.title: Six Weeks, Six Centuries
story.kicker: A gym teacher's plan book gives six weeks to arts that took centuries to grow.
paragraphs: A plan book lies open on a desk in a high school gym office. One page is headed Combatives, Weeks 1 to 6. Down the left side the teacher has written six names: wrestling, boxing, judo, karate, fencing and taekwondo. Each name gets one week.

Each of those names carries a long past. Wrestling appears in the art of ancient Egypt and Greece. Fencing schools were chartered by rulers in Europe in the 1400s. Judo was founded in Tokyo in 1882, and taekwondo was named in Korea in the 1950s.

The plan book has no room for most of that. It lists dates for a skills test, a grade and a permission slip. It does not list the masters, rule books, clubs and nations that shaped each art. A school unit is built for a semester, not for a family tree of teachers.

Schools did not invent this habit. Armies, gymnastics halls and college gyms packed fighting arts into short courses for more than two hundred years. They did it for fitness, for war and for school credit. Their records show what each short course kept and what it left out.
story.think: What might a student lose if six arts from six places each get only one week?

lessons.title: Ling's Institute in Stockholm
lessons.mainIdea: Per Henrik Ling built a Swedish school system of gymnastics in 1813 that placed fencing inside a larger plan for the body.
reading: Per Henrik Ling was born in Sweden in 1776. He worked as a fencing master at Lund University in the early 1800s. In 1813 he founded the Royal Central Institute of Gymnastics in Stockholm. The Swedish state paid for it and trained teachers there. Its graduates taught in schools and army units across Sweden.

Ling divided his *gymnastics* into four branches: educational, military, medical and aesthetic. *Military gymnastics* included fencing with swords and training with bayonets. Fencing was no longer a separate art with its own masters. It became one branch of a national program for soldiers and students.

Ling died in 1839, and his students carried the system abroad. In 1889 the Boston Normal School of Gymnastics opened to train American women as teachers of the Swedish system. A *normal school* is a college that trains teachers. Swedish gymnastics then spread into many American public schools.

words.d: in the 1800s, a broad word for planned exercise of the whole body, taught in schools and armies
the branch of Ling's system that trained soldiers, including fencing and bayonet training
a college that trains teachers

look.prompt: How many years passed between the Stockholm institute and the Boston school?

choices: outside the system as a separate art

choices: a school with no special rules
check.why: A normal school trains teachers, like the Boston school that taught Swedish gymnastics.

lessons.title: The Turners Cross the Ocean
lessons.mainIdea: German Turner clubs began in Berlin in 1811, came to American cities with immigrants after 1848, and pushed gymnastics into public schools.
reading: In 1811 Friedrich Ludwig Jahn opened an outdoor exercise ground at the Hasenheide in Berlin. It was called a *Turnplatz*, a place for Turnen, the German word for gymnastics. Jahn linked exercise to German national feeling after Napoleon's armies had defeated Prussia. Prussia banned Turnen in 1820 because rulers feared its politics, and the ban lasted until 1842.

The revolutions of 1848 in the German states failed. Many who took part fled to the United States, and Americans called them *Forty-Eighters*. They founded Turner clubs, called a *Turnverein*. The first in the United States opened in Cincinnati in 1848, and the Chicago Turngemeinde followed in 1852.

A Turner hall held gymnastics, fencing, singing, lectures and a library. Turners in Midwestern cities, including Chicago, pressed school boards to add gymnastics to public schools. They also trained many of the first gym teachers. Their clubs treated exercise as one part of a free citizen's education.

words.d: a German outdoor exercise ground, like the one Jahn opened in Berlin in 1811
Germans who took part in the failed revolutions of 1848 and moved to the United States
a German or German American gymnastics club

look.title: A Turner Hall Program
look.text: Picture a program board in a Chicago Turner hall in the 1880s. Monday: boys' gymnastics class. Tuesday: fencing club. Wednesday: men's chorus. Thursday: lecture on public schools. Saturday: children's class taught by a hall teacher who later works for the city schools.
look.prompt: Which items on the board show that Turners saw exercise as part of a larger education?

check.q: Who opened the Turnplatz at the Hasenheide in Berlin in 1811?
check.why: Jahn opened the Hasenheide ground; Ling worked in Sweden.

check.q: Why did Prussia ban Turnen in 1820?
check.why: Turnen was tied to national political feeling, which Prussian rulers feared.

check.q: Who were the Forty-Eighters?
choices: the first 48 members of a Chicago club

soldiers in the Civil War draft
check.why: The name comes from the revolutions of 1848 in the German states.

lessons.title: Harvard Measures Its Students
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s American colleges turned exercise into a measured school subject, and teachers formed a national association in 1885.
reading: In 1879 Dudley Allen Sargent became director of the new Hemenway Gymnasium at Harvard College. He measured each student's height, weight and strength when they arrived. Then he wrote a personal exercise plan for each one. Measuring the body in this way is called *anthropometry*.

Sargent designed his own exercise machines with weights and pulleys, and other colleges copied them. His records turned exercise into something a college could chart, grade and compare. That idea of a graded school subject shaped *physical education* for the next century.

In 1885 William G. Anderson gathered teachers in Brooklyn to found the American Association for the Advancement of Physical Education. The group grew into today's *SHAPE America*. A national association could write standards, hold meetings and publish journals. Fencing and wrestling in schools would now be judged by those standards, not by the old masters of each art.

words.d: measuring the human body, such as height, weight and strength
exercise and sport taught as a graded school subject
the national group of physical education teachers that grew from an association founded in 1885

look.title: Two Ways to Judge a Fencer

look.prompt: What does each way of judging value? Which one fits a school better, and why?

check.why: Sargent directed the Hemenway Gymnasium; Anderson founded the 1885 association.

check.q: What is anthropometry?
choices: a kind of school permission slip
check.why: Anthropometry means measuring the body, as Sargent did with each student.

check.q: What did the association founded in Brooklyn in 1885 later become?
check.why: The American Association for the Advancement of Physical Education grew into SHAPE America.

lessons.title: Training Camps of 1917
lessons.mainIdea: When the United States entered World War I in 1917, the Army taught boxing to huge groups of recruits as fitness and morale training.
reading: The United States entered World War I in April 1917. The Army had to train hundreds of thousands of new soldiers in months. The War Department formed the *Commission on Training Camp Activities* that same year. Raymond Fosdick led it. Congress passed a draft law, the Selective Service Act, in May 1917.

The commission ran sports, games and entertainment in the camps. Boxing got special attention because officers believed it built fitness and courage. Boxing coaches, including some professional fighters, taught large groups of recruits at the same time. Camp newspapers reported bouts between units.

Army boxing looked very different from a boxing club. A club let a boxer learn under one trainer for years. A camp gave thousands of men a short course before they shipped to France. After the war, many of those men came home as boxing fans, and the sport grew in American cities in the 1920s.

words.d: a War Department body formed in 1917 to run sports and recreation in Army camps
a newly enlisted soldier
the spirit and confidence of a group, such as soldiers

look.title: Club and Camp
look.text: A boxing club in 1910 has one trainer, a few members and years to learn. An Army camp in 1917 has one coach, hundreds of recruits on a field, and a few weeks before the troops sail to France.
look.prompt: What does each setting make possible? What does each one leave out?

check.q: When did the United States enter World War I?
check.why: The United States declared war in April 1917.

check.q: Who led the Commission on Training Camp Activities?
check.why: Raymond Fosdick led the commission formed in 1917.

check.q: Why did Army officers favor boxing in the camps?
choices: It was required by the Olympic rules
It needed no coaches at all
They believed it built fitness and courage
check.why: Officers saw boxing as a way to build fitness and courage in recruits.

lessons.title: Tunney and the AEF Title
lessons.mainIdea: Gene Tunney won a boxing title in the American Expeditionary Forces in 1919 and became world heavyweight champion in 1926.
reading: The *American Expeditionary Forces*, or AEF, were the U.S. troops sent to Europe in World War I. After the fighting ended in November 1918, many soldiers waited months in France to go home. The Army held sports tournaments to keep them busy. Boxing was one of the largest.

Gene Tunney was a young Marine from New York. In 1919 he won the light heavyweight championship of the AEF in Paris. The title made his name known to soldiers and sportswriters. He turned his wartime fame into a professional career. He fought as a professional for the rest of the 1920s.

In 1926 Tunney defeated Jack Dempsey in Philadelphia to win the world *heavyweight* title. In 1927 they fought again at Soldier Field in Chicago. That rematch is remembered for the long count, when a referee's delay in counting became a famous argument. Tunney retired as champion in 1928.

words.d: the U.S. troops sent to Europe in World War I, called the AEF
the heaviest weight class in boxing
the famous delay in a referee's count in the 1927 Tunney and Dempsey fight in Chicago

rows: Wins the AEF light heavyweight title

look.cite: Standard boxing records; U.S. Marine Corps history
look.prompt: How many years passed between Tunney's Army title and his world title?

check.q: What title did Gene Tunney win in Paris in 1919?
check.why: Tunney won the AEF light heavyweight title in 1919; the world title came in 1926.

check.q: Where was the 1927 Tunney and Dempsey rematch held?
choices: Madison Square Garden in New York
check.why: The rematch was at Soldier Field; the first fight was in Philadelphia.

check.q: Why did the Army hold boxing tournaments in France after November 1918?
choices: The war was still being fought
The Olympics were held in the camps

check.why: After the fighting ended, the Army used sports to occupy troops waiting to sail home.

lessons.title: Pre-Flight Schools, 1942
lessons.mainIdea: In World War II the Navy trained future pilots at college campuses, where boxing and wrestling were required parts of the course.
reading: In 1942 the U.S. Navy opened four *pre-flight schools* on college campuses. They were at the University of Iowa, the University of North Carolina, the University of Georgia and Saint Mary's College in California. Cadets spent months there before they began flight training.

Navy officer Tom Hamilton, a former football coach, shaped the program. Cadets took swimming, football, boxing, wrestling and hand-to-hand combat. The Navy hired college coaches as officers to teach them. Each school also fielded a football team that played college teams, such as the Iowa Pre-Flight Seahawks.

The pre-flight schools used college gyms, pools and coaches for a war goal. A cadet might box and wrestle for a few months and never step on a mat again. Yet thousands of young men left these schools with a short, graded course in combat sports on their records.

words.d: a World War II Navy school that trained cadets in fitness and study before flight training
a young person in training to become an officer
fighting without guns, taught to soldiers and sailors as a military skill

check.why: Cadets trained in fitness and study there before they learned to fly.

check.q: Who shaped the Navy pre-flight program?
check.why: Tom Hamilton, a former football coach, shaped the program.

lessons.title: Where the Word Combatives Comes From
lessons.mainIdea: Combatives is a military word; the U.S. Army used it for its field manuals and built a new program around it in the early 2000s.
reading: *Combatives* is a word from military training. It means fighting skills taught to soldiers as one package, not as separate arts with their own lineages. The U.S. Army printed a *field manual* called FM 21-150, Combatives, in several editions in the twentieth century. A field manual is an official Army handbook.

In the late 1990s Matt Larsen, a soldier in the 75th Ranger Regiment, began building a new program. It drew on Brazilian jiu-jitsu, wrestling, boxing, judo and Muay Thai. The Army set up a combatives school at Fort Benning, Georgia. In 2002 it published a new manual, FM 3-25.150, Combatives.

The Army program became the *Modern Army Combatives Program*. It borrowed pieces from arts with long histories in Brazil, Japan, Thailand and elsewhere. It kept what served soldiers and left out the rooms, rituals and teachers of each art. School PE units later borrowed the word combatives from this military use.

words.d: a military word for fighting skills taught to soldiers as one package
an official U.S. Army handbook, named with FM and a number
the U.S. Army's training program built in the late 1990s and early 2000s

look.title: An Army Manual's Title Page
look.text: The 2002 manual is titled Combatives and numbered FM 3-25.150. It is issued by Headquarters, Department of the Army, and it replaces the earlier manual FM 21-150.

choices: one Japanese art with a single founder

check.why: Combatives is a military word for a package of fighting skills.

check.q: Which manual did the Army publish in 2002?
check.why: FM 3-25.150 appeared in 2002 and replaced FM 21-150.

check.q: What did the Army program leave out when it borrowed from other arts?
check.why: The program kept what served soldiers and left out each art's rooms, rituals and teachers.

lessons.title: Title IX and the Mixed PE Class
lessons.mainIdea: Rules written under Title IX in 1975 made most PE classes coeducational, while letting schools group students by sex during contact sports.
reading: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 bans sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money. In 1975 the federal government issued the *regulations* that explained how schools must follow it. Regulations are detailed rules written by a government agency to carry out a law.

One regulation covered physical education classes. Schools could no longer run separate PE classes for boys and girls. A class had to be *coeducational*, meaning open to students of both sexes. Before this, many schools taught wrestling only to boys and dance only to girls.

The rule had an exception. During wrestling, boxing, rugby, ice hockey, football, basketball and other *contact sports*, a school could group students by sex inside the class. Teams for school sports follow a different regulation. The PE class rule is about who may enroll, not who may join a varsity team.

words.d: detailed rules written by a government agency to carry out a law
open to students of both sexes together
a sport whose main activity involves bodily contact, such as wrestling or football

lessons.title: A Waiver a Court Refused
lessons.mainIdea: In 1988 the Washington Supreme Court ruled that a public school could not make students sign away their right to sue before joining school sports.
reading: A *waiver*, also called a release, is a paper in which a person gives up a right to sue if they are hurt. In the 1980s, school districts in Washington State asked students and parents to sign waivers before sports. Families who refused could not play. Two families challenged the practice.

In 1988 the Washington Supreme Court decided the case *Wagenblast v. Odessa School District*. The court ruled that the school waivers were not enforceable. It said school sports are an important public service and families have little choice but to sign. The court used factors from a 1963 California case, Tunkl v. Regents of the University of California.

The ruling did not ban school sports or change how teachers ran practice. It said a school still owes its students a *duty of care*, the legal duty to act with reasonable safety. A signed paper could not erase that duty. Courts in other states have looked to the case in later disputes.

words.d: a paper in which a person gives up a right to sue if they are hurt
a 1988 Washington Supreme Court case that refused to enforce school sports waivers
the legal duty to act with reasonable safety toward others

look.title: Two Signatures
look.text: A private karate club asks an adult to sign a release before joining. A public high school asks a parent to sign the same kind of release before a student may join the wrestling team. In the second case, the student has no other public team to choose.
look.prompt: Using the 1988 ruling, why might a court treat these two papers differently?

check.q: What is a waiver?
choices: a paper giving up a right to sue if hurt

a rule that allows mixed classes
check.why: A waiver, or release, gives up a right to sue.

check.q: What did the court decide in Wagenblast v. Odessa School District in 1988?
choices: School sports waivers were not enforceable

check.why: The Washington Supreme Court refused to enforce the school waivers.

check.q: What does duty of care mean?
choices: a student's duty to attend class

check.why: Duty of care is the legal duty to act with reasonable safety toward others.

lessons.title: Illinois Answers Molitor
lessons.mainIdea: After a 1959 court case ended blanket school immunity in Illinois, the state passed the Tort Immunity Act of 1965 to set new limits on lawsuits.
reading: For many years, Illinois courts held that school districts could not be sued for injuries. This idea is called *governmental immunity*. In 1959 the Illinois Supreme Court decided Molitor v. Kaneland Community Unit District No. 302. A student hurt in a school bus crash in Kane County had sued the district.

The court ended the old immunity for school districts in that case. School districts across Illinois now faced lawsuits over injuries on buses, playgrounds and in gyms. The General Assembly responded. In 1965 it passed the Local Governmental and Governmental Employees *Tort Immunity Act*.

A *tort* is a harm one person causes another that a court can remedy with money. The 1965 act gave schools and their workers protection in many cases, but not all. It left them open to suits for conduct that was willful and wanton, meaning reckless disregard for safety. Illinois gyms and wrestling rooms still work under this law.

words.d: the old rule that a government body, such as a school district, could not be sued
a harm one person causes another that a court can remedy, usually with money
the 1965 Illinois law that sets when local governments and schools can be sued
conduct that shows reckless disregard for other people's safety
